analogy.p: Think of each carbon atom as a LEGO brick with exactly four connection studs. A hydrocarbon is a model built from only two brick types: the carbon brick (four studs) and a tiny hydrogen cap (one stud). An alkane is like a chain of carbon bricks where every free stud has been capped with hydrogen, so no stud is left open: that is 'saturated'. Crude oil is like a giant mixed bag of chains of every length thrown together, not glued to each other. The analogy breaks down because real bonds are shared electrons, not studs, and real molecules are three-dimensional and constantly moving.

bullets: Crude oil is **not** a pure substance: it is a thick, dark liquid that is a **mixture of many different compounds**.
It is described as **ancient biomass**: living material (mainly tiny sea creatures called plankton) that died millions of years ago.
It is **finite** because it forms over **millions of years**, far slower than we use it.
It is **non-renewable**: once the reserves are used up they cannot be replaced in a useful time.
It is found trapped in porous rock underground and is brought up by **drilling**.
Natural gas (mostly methane) is formed in the same way and is often found with crude oil.
Exam point: write 'finite' or 'non-renewable', not 'it will run out soon' on its own.
core.h: Crude oil: what it is and why it is finite
core.p: **Crude oil** is a **finite resource** found in rocks. It is the remains of ancient **biomass**, mainly **plankton**, that was buried in mud. Finite means it will run out, because it takes millions of years to form and we are using it far faster than it is being made. Because it is not replaced on a human timescale it is called **non-renewable**. Crude oil is the starting point for most petrol, diesel, kerosene and a huge range of plastics and other materials.

bullets: Step 1: **plankton** (tiny sea organisms) die and sink to the sea bed.
Step 2: their remains are **buried under mud and sediment** and more layers build up.
Step 3: **high temperature and pressure** act on the buried remains for **millions of years**.
Step 4: the remains slowly change into **crude oil** (and natural gas), which collects in porous rock.
Step 5: the oil is **drilled**, piped or shipped to a **refinery**.
Common 4-mark answer: ancient plankton / buried in mud / heat and pressure / millions of years.
Coal is also a fossil fuel but forms from ancient **plants**; do not confuse the two.
core.h: How crude oil was formed (step by step)
core.p: The mark scheme wants you to link the starting material, the conditions and the timescale. Plankton lived in ancient seas. When they died, their bodies sank and were buried under mud and sediment. Over **millions of years** the **heat and pressure** from the layers above, with no oxygen present to rot the remains away, slowly changed the organic material into crude oil. The oil became trapped in rock where it could be drilled. See the flow diagram below.

bullets: The compounds in crude oil are **not chemically bonded together**.
Each compound keeps its own **chemical properties** (for example, how it burns).
A mixture can be separated by **physical processes** (filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, **fractional distillation**, chromatography).
Crude oil has **no fixed boiling point**; it boils over a range of temperatures as the different molecules vaporise.
Crude oil is mostly hydrocarbons, but can include small amounts of other substances (such as compounds containing sulfur).
Link: a pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting or boiling point, a mixture does not (Atomic structure and the periodic table topic).
Link: mixtures and separation techniques are in Chemistry Paper 1 (4.1.1.2) but are applied here.
core.p: A **mixture** consists of two or more elements or compounds that are **not chemically combined**. Because the substances in crude oil are not bonded to each other, each keeps its own chemical properties and can be separated by **physical methods** such as distillation. Crude oil contains molecules with chains of different lengths, so different parts of the mixture have different boiling points. This is the whole reason that fractional distillation (next topic) works.

bullets: Definition: **a compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only**.
The atoms are joined by **covalent bonds** (shared pairs of electrons), so hydrocarbons are **simple molecular** substances.
Examples: methane CH4, propane C3H8, ethene C2H4. Non-examples: ethanol C2H5OH (has O), carbon dioxide (no H).
Carbon always forms **4 covalent bonds** and hydrogen forms **1** in these molecules.
Hydrocarbons come in **chains of different lengths** (and also rings, although you do not need these).
Hydrocarbons are **non-polar**-type molecules and do not dissolve in water.
The word 'hydrocarbon' does **not** tell you whether the bonds are single or double: that is saturated versus unsaturated.
core.p: A **hydrocarbon** is a compound made of **hydrogen and carbon atoms only**. The name tells you exactly what is in it: hydro (hydrogen) and carbon. Any compound that contains another element, such as oxygen (as in ethanol) or chlorine, is **not** a hydrocarbon. Most of the compounds in crude oil are hydrocarbons, and these are the molecules that make good fuels because carbon and hydrogen both release energy when they are oxidised.

bullets: General formula: **CnH2n+2**, where n is the number of carbon atoms.
The name ending **-ane** tells you it is an alkane.
The first four: **methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10**.
Each member differs from the next by **one CH2 unit**.
All alkanes have **similar chemical properties** because they have the same bonds (all single C–C and C–H).
Physical properties such as **boiling point** change in a regular way as chain length increases.
Methane, ethane, propane and butane are **gases at room temperature**; longer alkanes are liquids and then waxy solids.
core.h: Alkanes: the main hydrocarbons in crude oil
core.p: Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil are hydrocarbons called **alkanes**. Alkanes are a **homologous series**: a family of compounds with the **same general formula**, similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties. All alkanes have names ending in **-ane**. The alkanes you must know first are methane, ethane, propane and butane, which have 1, 2, 3 and 4 carbon atoms.

bullets: Forwards: n = 5, H = 2 x 5 + 2 = 12, so the alkane is **C5H12** (pentane).
Forwards: n = 10, H = 22, so **C10H22** (decane).
Backwards: H = 26, then (26 − 2) ÷ 2 = 12, so **C12H26**.
If the H number is **not** 2n+2 the molecule is **not an alkane**: C4H8 (2n would be 8) fits CnH2n and is an alkene.
The H count is always **even** for an alkane (2n + 2 is even).
Why 2n+2? Each carbon in the middle of a chain has 2 H; the two end carbons each have 1 extra H.
Check: C20H42 is an alkane (2 x 20 + 2 = 42).
core.h: The general formula CnH2n+2 and how to use it
core.p: The general formula is a rule that links the number of hydrogen atoms to the number of carbon atoms. If a chain has **n** carbon atoms, it has **2n + 2** hydrogen atoms. To use it, double the carbon number and add two. You can also use it backwards: subtract 2 from the number of hydrogen atoms and halve the answer to find n. Always test your answer by checking that every carbon has four bonds in total.

bullets: **Saturated** = contains **only single bonds** between carbon atoms (no C=C).
A single covalent bond is a **shared pair of electrons** between two atoms.
Carbon is in Group 4, so it has **4 outer electrons** and forms **4 bonds**; hydrogen has 1 outer electron and forms **1 bond**.
Because every carbon already has its four bonds, saturated molecules cannot add extra atoms to the chain.
Compare **unsaturated** hydrocarbons (alkenes) which contain a **C=C double bond** (see the later topic).
Saturated is **not** the same as 'full of hydrogen' in the exam: say 'only single bonds, no double bonds'.
Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water (alkenes do): this is the test for saturated vs unsaturated, covered later.
core.p: Alkanes are **saturated** hydrocarbons. Saturated means that every carbon-carbon bond is a **single covalent bond**, so the molecule contains the **maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms** and has **no C=C double bonds**. Each carbon atom has four electrons in its outer shell and shares each one in a covalent bond, so it forms four bonds. Each hydrogen shares its one electron and forms one bond. This is why a carbon atom in an alkane always has four lines around it in a displayed formula.

bullets: **Methane CH4**: one C with four H. 'meth-' = 1 carbon.
**Ethane C2H6**: H3C–CH3, 'eth-' = 2 carbons.
**Propane C3H8**: CH3–CH2–CH3, 'prop-' = 3 carbons.
**Butane C4H10**: CH3–CH2–CH2–CH3, 'but-' = 4 carbons.
Displayed formula: draw every C, every H and every bond as a line (see diagram). 'Structural' formulae like CH3CH2CH3 are shorter versions.
Count check: each C has exactly **4** lines, each H has exactly **1** line.
Extension names: pentane C5H12, hexane C6H14, heptane C7H16, octane C8H18 (pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-).
core.h: Names, formulae and displayed formulae of the first four alkanes
core.p: You must be able to recall each name and molecular formula and draw the **displayed formula**, which shows **every atom and every bond**. Methane has one carbon with four hydrogens around it. Ethane has two carbons joined by a single bond with three hydrogens on each. Propane has three carbons in a chain, and butane has four. Notice that the carbon chain is drawn as a straight line but the real molecule is not flat or straight; at GCSE the flat drawing is accepted.

bullets: Same **general formula** (CnH2n+2 for alkanes).
Successive members differ by **CH2**.
**Similar chemical properties** because they react in the same way (e.g. all burn in oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water).
Physical properties change gradually: **boiling point and viscosity increase** with chain length.
The first four alkanes are gases; the middle ones are liquids; the long ones are solids at room temperature.
The same idea applies to alkenes (CnH2n), alcohols and carboxylic acids later in the course.
Exam phrase: 'same general formula, similar chemical properties, gradual trend in physical properties'.
core.h: Homologous series: what they have in common
core.p: A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds with the **same functional group**, the **same general formula**, **similar chemical properties** and a **gradual change in physical properties**. Alkanes are the homologous series you meet first. Knowing the idea lets you predict the properties of a molecule you have never seen: if you know how propane burns, you know how octane will burn. Physical properties such as boiling point depend on molecule size, so they change step by step along the series.

bullets: Write the symbol **C** for each carbon and **H** for each hydrogen; no dots or crosses are needed in a displayed formula.
Draw **one straight line per single bond**; do not forget the C–H bonds.
Check each carbon has **4 lines**; check each hydrogen has **1 line**.
Count the totals and confirm they match **CnH2n+2**.
For butane, a straight chain of four carbons with H above, below and on both ends is right.
Do not draw a hydrogen joined to **another hydrogen** or a carbon with a hydrogen attached by two lines in an alkane.
In 'draw the displayed formula of propane' for 2 marks: 1 mark carbon chain, 1 mark all H correctly placed.
core.h: Drawing displayed formulae: rules and checks
core.p: Examiners are strict about displayed formulae because they test whether you understand covalent bonding. Draw each atom with its symbol and join atoms with straight lines, one line for each single bond. Every carbon must have exactly four bonds and every hydrogen exactly one. A common slip is to leave out an H or to give a carbon five bonds. After drawing, count the atoms and match them to the molecular formula as a final check.

bullets: Fuels for transport, heating and electricity generation.
Feedstock for making **polymers (plastics)**, solvents, lubricants and detergents.
Crude oil is a **finite** resource, so sustainability is a concern.
Burning hydrocarbons releases **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas (Atmosphere topic).
The next two topics explain how crude oil is **separated** (fractional distillation) and how large molecules are **cracked**.
Higher tier link: explaining trends in boiling point uses **intermolecular forces** (Bonding topic).
Fuel oils cannot be used in cars; the molecule length decides how a fraction can be used.
core.h: Why alkanes matter: fuels and feedstock
core.p: The hydrocarbons in crude oil are extremely useful. Many are burned as **fuels** because they release a large amount of energy when oxidised. Others are used as **feedstock** (the raw material) for the **petrochemical industry**, providing the starting materials for solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents. Because crude oil is finite, there is a drive to find alternatives such as biofuels and hydrogen, and to use oil more carefully.

bullets: **Bonding**: covalent bonding, simple molecular structures with weak intermolecular forces.
**Periodic table**: carbon is in Group 4 and forms four bonds.
**Energy changes**: combustion is exothermic.
**Atmosphere**: combustion makes CO2 and H2O; incomplete combustion makes CO and soot.
**Organic chemistry**: fractional distillation, cracking, alkenes, polymers.
**Resources**: finite resources and sustainability.
Higher tier: be ready to give reasoned explanations that link several of these ideas in 6-mark answers.
core.p: This topic ties together bonding, the periodic table, energy changes and the environment. The structure of an alkane comes from carbon being in Group 4 and forming four covalent bonds. The small size of the simplest alkanes explains why they are gases, and the way they burn connects to exothermic reactions and to the greenhouse effect. Good answers link ideas together instead of listing isolated facts.

exam: 'State' / 'give' (1 mark): one short fact, e.g. 'Hydrocarbons contain hydrogen and carbon only'.
'Describe how crude oil was formed' (3-4 marks): plankton died and were buried in mud, heat and pressure, millions of years. One mark per link in the chain.
'Define hydrocarbon' (1 mark): use the exact wording 'compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only' and the word 'only'.
'What does saturated mean?' (1 mark): 'contains only single carbon–carbon bonds' or 'no C=C double bonds'.
Formula questions: always show the working 2n + 2 so you can earn the method mark even if your arithmetic slips.
'Draw the displayed formula of ...' (1-2 marks): all atoms and all bonds; count 4 bonds on each C and 1 on each H.
'Explain why crude oil is a finite resource' (2 marks): forms very slowly (millions of years) and is used much faster than it forms.
'Why is crude oil a mixture?' (2 marks): different compounds not chemically bonded, so each keeps its own properties and they can be separated.
Do not say 'compound' for crude oil and avoid 'renewable'; both lose marks every year.
Use the data in the question: if given a formula, test it with CnH2n+2 to decide if it is an alkane.

mistakes.r: Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons that are not chemically bonded to each other.
It formed from the remains of ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud.
mistakes.w: Crude oil formed from dead dinosaurs.

mistakes.r: Hydrocarbons contain hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
mistakes.w: Hydrocarbons contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

mistakes.r: Saturated means it contains only single bonds (no C=C double bonds) between carbon atoms.
mistakes.w: Saturated means it is full of hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Butane is C4H10: use CnH2n+2 so 2 x 4 + 2 = 10.
Crude oil is finite/non-renewable because it takes millions of years to form, far slower than it is used.
mistakes.w: Crude oil is renewable because plankton is still dying.

mistakes.r: Every carbon has exactly four bonds and every hydrogen exactly one; all atoms and bonds must be shown.
mistakes.w: A carbon with five bonds, or an H left off, in a displayed formula.

mistakes.r: Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil are alkanes (saturated).
mistakes.w: Alkenes are the main hydrocarbons in crude oil.

summary: You must know that crude oil is a finite resource formed from the remains of ancient biomass (mainly plankton) and is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, most of which are alkanes. You need to define a hydrocarbon, recall the general formula CnH2n+2 for alkanes and know the names, formulae and displayed formulae of methane, ethane, propane and butane. Alkanes underpin fuels and the petrochemical industry, so this is the base for all of organic chemistry.

terms.d: A finite resource found in rocks, the remains of ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud; a mixture of many hydrocarbons.
A resource that will run out because it is used up faster than it is formed.
Cannot be replaced at the rate at which it is used; takes millions of years to form.
Living or recently living material, such as plankton, plants and animals.
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together; the substances keep their own properties.
A compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
A saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula CnH2n+2; names end in -ane.
A family of organic compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, with a gradual trend in physical properties.
Containing only single carbon–carbon bonds, so no C=C double bonds.
Containing at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C).
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
An algebraic formula for the members of a homologous series, e.g. CnH2n+2 for alkanes.
A diagram showing all the atoms in a molecule and all the covalent bonds as lines.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule, e.g. C3H8.
A raw material used as the starting point of an industrial process, e.g. in the petrochemical industry.

worked.q: An alkane has 7 carbon atoms. Work out its molecular formula and name. (2 marks)
An alkane has 22 hydrogen atoms in each molecule. How many carbon atoms does it have? (2 marks)

worked.ans: Crude oil formed from ancient plankton that died and was buried in mud. Over millions of years, heat and pressure changed the remains into crude oil, which became trapped in rocks.
worked.q: Describe how crude oil was formed. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: made from the remains of ancient biomass/plankton that died.
Mark 2: remains were buried under mud/sediment on the sea bed.
Mark 3: heat and pressure acted on the remains.
Mark 4: over millions of years, in the absence of oxygen, forming crude oil.
